EIP-0031: Untitled
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: eip, eip-0031, standards
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

### Contract template
Compilation of babel fee box smartcontracts for different tokens of interest will result in different P2S addresses, leading to each token having a unique corresponding ErgoTree and consequently a unique P2S babel fee box smartcontract address. To avoid having to rebuild the contract for each token, the implementer can use the following contract template, where the `{tokenId}` fragment must be replaced by the hexadecimal identifier of the token of interest.

```
100604000e20{tokenId}
```

### Output position

The position of the recreated Babel Box in transaction's outputs must be set as a context extension variable in the spending Babel Box.

1. Context variable `0`:
    * Type: `SInt`
    * Value: position of the recreated Babel Box in transaction's outputs

title: EIP-0031: Untitled
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: eip, eip-0031, standards
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

### Parameters
Parameters (creator’s public key and price) are specified via registers, meaning the resulting babel fee boxes from different creators will always belong to the same P2S address, which will improve their searchability.

1. Register `R4`:
    * Type: `SigmaProp`
    * Value: creator's public key
2. Register `R5`:
    * Type: `SLong`
    * Value: how much nanoErgs is the creator willing to pay for one babel token
3. Register `R6`:
    * Type: `SColl[Byte]`
    * Value: id of the Babel Box being spent by this
    * Only required for recreated boxes

Babel fee box creator is able to spent the babel box in any circumstances.

Other users on the other hand can spend this box as input to their transaction only when they also recreate it as output of their transaction with the very same `R4` and `R5` registers values together with `R6` as described above and insertion of a required amount of babel tokens (the amount of inserted babel tokens multiplied by the price specified in the R5 register has to be equal to or bigger than the amount of nanoErgs spent from the babel fee box).

Wallets implementation
--------------------------------------------

Wallet developers will need to decide whether they want to support EIP-0031 or not. If they do decide to support this standard, they should also decide on which tokens they want to support (this could be done based on user requirements – e.g. implementing big stablecoins or “meme” coins, etc.), as this could be more convenient than supporting all tokens.

As P2S addresses belonging to specific token of interest stay the same, these addresses could be easily “hardcoded” when supporting only a few tokens. If the developers decide to support any token, the previously mentioned smartcontract for each token which user holds should be compiled or "mounted" as described on ["Contract template"](#contract-template) subsection and the availability of Babel Fee boxes (UTXOs) for the specific tokens of interest in the blockchain should be subsequently checked.

The proposed babel fee smartcontract is quite general and does not impose much restriction for the transaction. It is therefore possible to transact some tokens while paying babel fees with another tokens, etc. 

Once the wallet finds a babel fee box which could be used to pay required transaction fees, it should calculate the required price for the transaction fee and present it to the user, so he can decide on using this particular option or not.

The wallet should also check current mempool and determine whether there exists someone who is currently trying to spend this specific babel fee box. In that case, the wallet should construct “chained” transaction (using the mempool’s transaction output (recreated babel fee output) as the new babel fee box input). This way, many transactions spending “the same” box could be chained and mined inside a single block. There can also occur a situation when the babel fee box owner is trying to spend his own box. In that case, the wallet should select another babel fee box, if available. 

Once the wallet successfully crafts and relays the transaction to the mempool, it MUST keep an eye on the transaction until it is mined. This is important because the wallet cannot prevent somebody else from trying to spend the exact same babel fee box as our user’s transaction is trying to spend. When there are two transactions trying to spend the same box, only one from them can be mined and therefore included in the blockchain, while the other one has to be recrafted with the new babel fee box and relayed again to the network. Such thing should occur rarely, but when it does, the wallet has to be able to handle the situation correctly while notifying the user that the transaction did not go through.

Reference implementations
--------------------------------------------
* [Nautilus Wallet implementation](https://github.com/capt-nemo429/nautilus-wallet/pull/82)
* [AppKit implementation](https://github.com/ergoplatform/ergo-appkit/pull/204)

title: EIP-0034: NFT Collection Standard
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: eip, eip-0034, standards
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Motivation 
NFT collections play a central role in the nowadays NFT ecosystem on all blockchains. It gives the ability to artists to organize their artworks and present them in a more meaningful way. It also can facilitate the use of other NFT features such as traits. As we'll present in this proposal, it can also enable more advanced features such as artist collaborations. These advanced features can get arbitrarily complex with the use of smart contracts.

title: EIP-0034: NFT Collection Standard
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: eip, eip-0034, standards
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Design
We consider collection NFTs as tokens! Following the design pattern in [artwork standard](eip-0024.md), we store the collection information in the issuer box rather than the issuance box so that this information is verifiable in smart contracts. The issuer box will contain all the collection information. Moreover, the issuance box will also contain some overlapping information for readability reasons.

An NFT will be considered as part of an already created collection if it follows the [artwork standard](eip-0024.md) and the collection NFT is present in the first input of the issuance transaction, also known as the royalty box or the issuer box.

There is no limitation on the number of issued tokens for a collection. One possible interpretation of such a feature is that artists can come together and create a collection. Each one of them will have one collection token which gives the right to them to add NFTs to that collection. We believe that with the use of smart contracts, more advanced usage of this flexibility will be discovered in the future.

title: EIP-0034: NFT Collection Standard
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: eip, eip-0034, standards
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## NFT Collection Standard
One of the main goals of this proposal is for the standard to be as future-proof as possible. To achieve that, some of the features we introduce here may not contain an extensive explanation of how to use them. This enables NFT developers to participate in the EIP and also plan for their tools. However, it comes with the downside that this EIP will be prone to backward-compatible extensions in the future. The following sections must be present in the issuer box of the collection.

### Collection standard version
Collection standard version must be present in `R4` as `Int`. This current standard version is `1`. This will enable future radical changes depending on the state of the NFT ecosystem.

### Collection Info
Collection info must be present in `R5` of the issuer box as `Coll[Coll[Byte]]`. The following is the needed info:
`["URL_TO_COLLECTION_LOGO", "URL_TO_COLLECTION_FEATURED_IMAGE","URL_TO_COLLECTION_BANNER_IMAGE", "COLLECTION_CATEGORY"]`.
 Name and description of collection must be present in the issuance box which follows [eip-004](eip-0004.md). 
The above structure must be encoded as `Coll[Coll[Byte]]`.

### Socials
Socials may be present in `R6` of the issuer box as `Coll[(Coll[Byte], Coll[Byte])]`. There are no restrictions on what socials to include. However, the name of the socials must be in lower case. The following is an example of socials that needs to be encoded as `Coll[(Coll[Byte], Coll[Byte])]`.

`[ ("twitter", "TWITTER_PROFILE_URL"), ("instagram", "INSTAGRAM_RPOFILE_URL") `

### Minting expiry
R7 of the issuer box must contain the expiry timestamp of minting in the collection as `Long`. After this timestamp is reached, no NFTs should be minted in the collection. Because tokens by default are not tied to smart contracts, this timestamp can not be forced. However, it can be verified by marketplaces. Moreover, the collection tokens can be locked within some smart contract that forces this feature. If there is no expiry, this must be set to `-1`.

### Additional information
R8 of the issuer box is reserved for additional information that might be needed in the future. The type of this register is `Coll[(Coll[Byte], Coll[Byte])]` and it is supposed to represent a json with the following format:

```json
{
  "key1": "value1",
  "key2": "value2",
  "...": "..."
}
```
Auction houses should add the information (i.e., "key", "value" and what it is intended to show) to this part before using it. Otherwise that piece of information is not considered to be part of the standard.

## Unlockable Content
Unlockable contents are files or other types of information that the artist reveals to the buyer when an NFT is sold (and/or some other conditions are satisfied). At the time of proposing this EIP, there are no known decentralized solutions to have unlockable contents. However, it is more than likely that we'll have solutions soon. So we anticipate that this EIP will get updated by using the remaining registers to have this feature.

# content > reference > eips

Tweaking Difficulty Adjustment Algorithm
==========================================

* Author: kushti
* Status: Implmented
* Created: 23-Sep-2022
* Last edited: 02-Oct-2022
* License: CC0
* Forking: hard-fork needed 

Motivation 
----------

Difficulty adjustment (also, readjustment) algorithm tries to stabilize averate time to generate a block by changing difficulty of solving a Proof-of-Work puzzle by observing difficulties and timestamps of historical blocks. First Proof-of-Work cryptocurrency, Bitcoin, used simplest lienar difficulty recalculation[1], with some limits for it, such as a difficulty never be changed by more than a factor of 4 either way to prevent large changes. 

Bitcoin's difficulty readjustment works more or less well since only dedicated and so loyal mining hardware working on PoW puzzlez. However, in other environments different issues were observed with it, including coin hopping. Thus different solutions to coin hopping appeared, inluding using a least squares method based predictive algorithm [3] as done in Ergo currently.

The Ergo's algorithm works well in most cases, inluding huge price drops, 100x initial difficulty misestimation during mainnet launch, and so on. However, current simplified and limitless version of algorithm is bumpy. Big influx of mining hashrate over multiple epochs, especially with super-linear hashrate growth over time may result in huge spike of difficulty. Similarly, few slow epochs may cause huge drop. Also, for dapps and other applications it would be desirable to make difficulty readjustment more reactive (currently, readjustment takes place every 1024 blocks, and 8 epochs, so about two weeks normally, are considered).   

Related Work
------------

To prevent disastrous effects of hopping, widespread approach (see e.g. https://read.cash/@jtoomim/bch-upgrade-proposal-use-asert-as-the-new-daa-1d875696 ) is to use weighted averaging functions over past epochs which do prefer last epochs.
Hovewer, in case of natural hashrate migration such functions will likely be lagging (in opposite to proactive nature of predictive least square method). 

Proposed Changes
----------------

We propose to make current difficulty readjustment more reactive and smoother by shortening epoch length, amplifying weight of the last epoch and put some limits on difficulty change as follows.

1. Epoch length to be set to 128 blocks. 
2. We calculate *predictive* difficulty according to 8 epochs 128 blocks each and *classic* difficulty as done in Bitcoin. 
We limit predictive difficulty change so that it never be changed by more than 50% per epoch. Then we took average from classic and predictive difficulties. 
3. We limit change so that difficulty never be changed by more than 50% per epoch.


Simulations
-----------

Previous simulations [4,5] are based on observing historical data so ignoring the fact that miners will behave differently in the presence of different difficulty adjustment method.

Thus we made playground simulating random price walking in uptrend or downtrend. In a simulation, a blockchain is being mined by rational hashpower only. Hashrate is looking at current price and diffuculty. We assume that price and difficulty are changed at the same time, and then hashrate is moving in or out, which is affecting average block generation time *t*. We may assume then that *t = d * c / p*, so average block generation time *t* is proportinal to difficulty *d* and inversely proportional to price *p*. Fixing *t* (which is set to target block generation time, so 2 minutes), *d* and *p* at the beginning of the experiment, we can evaluate *c*. Then on each step we are randomly changing *p* and, according to difficulty from the previous epoch, we can get average block generation time for the new epoch. To have a trend in price, we are changing *p* by adding (or subtracting) a random value with fixed average, and also adding a random fluctuation. 

Test results:

* if price growth is up to 5% per epoch, and possible fluctuation (up or down) is up to 10%:

*Bitcoin DAA*: total error: 158841, max delay: 133
*Current DAA*: total error: 189403, max delay: 151
*Proposed DAA: total error: 163893, max delay: 141 


* if no price growth, and possible fluctuation (up or down) is up to 25% (so price is jumping up and down like crazy):

*Bitcoin DAA*: total error: 393770, max delay: 161
*Current DAA*: total error: 528003, max delay: 224
*Proposed DAA: total error: 429667, max delay: 193 

* if average price growth is up 2% per epoch (max delay missed as it is 120s max for all the options):

*Bitcoin DAA*: total error: 30409
*Current DAA*: total error: 19111
*Proposed DAA: total error: 20691

* if average price growth is up 10% per epoch (max delay missed as it is 120s max for all the options):

Total error here is sum of differences between observed block generation time and target (120 s). The less total error, the better.

As we can see, proposed DAA as well as current one is working better during trends, and also in case of 1-epoch coin hopping, and proposed DAA softens swings better than current one. 

Activation
----------

It is possible to activate EIP-37 after block #843,776 and before block #851,969 . For activation, 232 or more votes for activation required in the last 256 blocks, with voting checked every 128 blocks (for blocks which height % 128 == 1), and immediate activation once threshold is met. 

Implementation
--------------

Proposed difficulty adjustment algorithm and its activation procedure are implemented in the reference protocol client 4.0.100, all the newer versions support them as well [6]. 


References
----------

1. BitcoinWiki. Difficulty in Mining https://en.bitcoinwiki.org/wiki/Difficulty_in_Mining
2. Bitcoin Wiki. Target https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Target#When_does_the_target_change_next.3F
3. Meshkov D., Chepurnoy A., Jansen M. Short paper: Revisiting difficulty control for blockchain systems
4. jtoomim BCH upgrade proposal: Use ASERT as the new DAA https://read.cash/@jtoomim/bch-upgrade-proposal-use-asert-as-the-new-daa-1d875696
5. Ergo Developers. DifficultyControlSimulator.scala https://github.com/ergoplatform/ergo/blob/0af9dd9d8846d672c1e2a77f8ab29963fa5acd1e/src/test/scala/org/ergoplatform/tools/DifficultyControlSimulator.scala

# EIP-39 Monotonic box creation height rule

* Author: MrStahlfelge
* Status: Proposed
* Created: 05-Oct-2022
* Implemented: Implemented
* Last edited: 12-Oct-2022
* License: CC0
* Forking: Soft-fork

title: EIP-0039: EIP-39 Monotonic box creation height rule
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: eip, eip-0039, standards
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Motivation

Storage rent is applied to boxes with an age of 4 years or more. The age of the box is determined
by current block height and the boxes self-reported creation height. The box can be spent by miners when 
the following expression is true:

preHeader.height - box.creationHeight > 30 * 24 * 365 * 4

Boxes self-report their creation height. While there is an upper limit set by the current block height, boxes 
reporting a lower creation height are allowed to be used in transactions. That means that boxes with creationHeight 0 
can be created, and can be spent 
by miners immediately after block 1,051,200. This is especially a problem for contracts anyone can spend and 
create transactions on. Outboxes can be created with a creation height far in the past unintentional or maliciously,
leading to a complete spending and token burn in worst case.

Contracts can be hardened to disallow this by checking their outboxes creation height. However, this had to 
be done for every single contract on its own. That's why we suggest to add a check on protocol level.

title: EIP-0039: EIP-39 Monotonic box creation height rule
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: eip, eip-0039, standards
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Suggestion

Suggestion to solve this problem on protocol level is to introduce a monotonic creation height rule as follows:

For every transaction that is submitted to the network, it should be validated if the following expression is satisfied:

    val highestInputBoxHeight = INPUTS.maxOf { input: Box => input.creationHeight }
    OUTPUTS.allOf { output: Box => output.creationHeight >= highestInputBoxHeight }

or in spoken words

> All creation heights of output boxes of a transaction must be equal or higher than the highest 
> creation height of the transaction's input boxes.

## Description
This EIP defines a data format for Reduced Transaction which can be used:
- to enable interoperation between an online dApp and a wallet app for creating, signing and sending Ergo transactions
- to serialize reduced transaction to QR code for scanning by a wallet app
- to serialize reduced transaction to JSON for using in Ergo node API

title: EIP-0043: EIP-43: Reduced Transaction
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: eip, eip-0043, standards
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Background And Motivation

In the Ergo's eUTXO model a box can be protected by an arbitrary complex
contract (aka spending condition) and the spending transaction should satisfy
that condition by adding required context variables, creating expected number of
outputs with specific registers etc. i.e. a special data structure called
`Context`. 

Say we want to sign a new transaction. The Context should be created for each input of the
transaction and then passed to the Prover which will generate a signature for that input.
See [general overview of signing and
verification](https://github.com/ScorexFoundation/sigmastate-interpreter#sigma-language-background)
process in Ergo for details.

In general, the Context represents the current state of the blockchain and includes
current header, previous 10 headers, current height etc. This data can be retrieved from
blockchain nodes. This is possible on Hot Wallet device - a device with a network
connection, but is not possible on [Cold Wallet](eip-0019.md) device (where there is no
network connection).

At the same time the prover (which generates a signature for the transaction) need to know
both the Context data _and_ the private keys, which are stored on the Cold Wallet device,
and so the Prover must run on the Cold Wallet device.

And that is the problem, we cannot transfer unsigned transaction along with all the
contexts for each input to the Cold Wallet via QR codes. QR codes have limit of 4K bytes
on the maximum size of serialized data. Even simplest transactions when serialized with
required Contexts will exceed this limit.

title: EIP-0043: EIP-43: Reduced Transaction
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: eip, eip-0043, standards
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Reduced Transaction data

Here we introduce a new data structure and serialization format called
`ReducedTransaction`.

```
ReducedTransaction:
  - unsignedTx: UnsignedTransaction
  - reducedInputs: Seq[ReducedInputData]
  - txCost: Int

UnsignedTransaction:
  - inputs: Seq[UnsignedInput],
  - dataInputs: Seq[DataInput],
  - outputCandidates: Seq[ErgoBoxCandidate]

UnsignedInput:
  - boxId: BoxId
  - extension: ContextExtension

ReducedInputData:
- reductionResult: ReductionResult

ReductionResult:
  - value: SigmaBoolean
  - cost: Long
```

Thus, the `ReducedTransaction` instance contains unsigned transaction augmented with
one `ReductionResult` for each `UnsignedInput`.

Note that `UnsignedInput` object doesn't contain `ergoTree`, `additionalTokens`,
`additionalRegisters` and other properties of
[ErgoBox](https://github.com/ScorexFoundation/sigmastate-interpreter/blob/4533b6a7ae86ada20f3136c70a67a920ae7c43e1/sigmastate/src/main/scala/org/ergoplatform/ErgoBox.scala#L51)
which are necessary to perform
[ErgoTree](https://github.com/ScorexFoundation/sigmastate-interpreter/blob/1a1b003bc30e490d8b5af30e7670227e54e682c2/sigmastate/src/main/scala/sigmastate/Values.scala#L1014)
reduction and which are part of the
[Context](https://github.com/ScorexFoundation/sigmastate-interpreter/blob/e5127f6743db824f7280881cd5c4ecd336075e2f/sigmastate/src/main/scala/org/ergoplatform/ErgoLikeContext.scala#L51)
data structure required by the
[prove](https://github.com/ScorexFoundation/sigmastate-interpreter/blob/f24833d8d4572d77e4a93e5b69360335cb2d7dc1/sigmastate/src/main/scala/sigmastate/interpreter/ProverInterpreter.scala#L104)
method to generate a proof (aka signature).

This is because those context data is not required to generate proof
once ErgoTree is reduced to ReductionResult containing sigma proposition.

title: EIP-0043: EIP-43: Reduced Transaction
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: eip, eip-0043, standards
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Data Formats

### ReducedTransaction

ReducedTransaction is serialized to bytes array in the format described below. Note, field
names are not serialized.

| Field Name      | Format              | Description                                       |
|-----------------|---------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| `messageSize`   | `VLQ(UInt)`         | Number of bytes in the messageToSign of the transaction |
| `messageToSign` | `Bytes`             | serialized bytes of the unsignedTx.messageToSign  |
| `reducedInputs` | `ReductionResult*` | serialized reduced inputs                         |
| `txCost`        | `VLQ(UInt)`        | transaction cost according to the prover          |

Note, the number of reduced inputs is serialized as part of the `messageToSign`.

### ReductionResult

Reduction result is obtained for each input of the original unsigned transaction.

| Field Name | Format         | Description                                                         |
|------------|----------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `value`    | `SigmaBoolean` | serialized sigma proposition, see section 5.2.2 in [2](#references) |
| `cost`     | `VLQ(ULong)`   | cost accumulated during reduction of the input's ErgoTree           |

title: EIP-0044: Arbitrary Data Signing Standard
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: eip, eip-0044, standards
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Requirements

- `R1` - Secure: signing process must prevent known attack vectors;
- `R2` - Verifiable: messages must have verifiable encoded representations;
- `R3` - Hardware wallet-friendly: message representation must be small enough to fit well in hardware wallet devices' screens, and the signing process must be as resource-efficient as possible.

title: EIP-0044: Arbitrary Data Signing Standard
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: eip, eip-0044, standards
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Encoding

To meet requirements `R2`, an encoding scheme becomes necessary. This document proposes an extension of the current Ergo addresses codeset.

Currently, we have the following setup:

- `1`: `P2PK` - Pay to Public Key
- `2`: `P2SH` - Pay to Script Hash
- `3`: `P2S` - Pay to Script

This document proposes a new address type code:

- `4`: `ADH` - Arbitrary Data Hash

Using the hashed data instead of the actual data bytes allows for shorter text representations and meets requirement `R3` for representation shortness and resource efficiency.

### Pseudocode implementation

Message encoding follows the same steps as regular addresses encoding, it mush have a head byte, a body and a checksum.

```ts
const addressCode = 4; // 4 = ADH - Arbitrary Data Hash

const headByte = [Network.Mainnet + addressCode];
const dataHash = blake2b256(dataBytes);
const body = concat(headByte, dataHash);
const checksum = blake2b256(body).subarray(0, 4);

const encodedRepresentation = base58(concat(body, checksum));
```

title: EIP-0044: Arbitrary Data Signing Standard
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: eip, eip-0044, standards
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Signing

The data signing process is done similarly to a regular transaction signing, basically a prover takes the data bytes and uses a private key to sign it. But sending data directly to the prover can lead to some known security issues, namely:

- `AV1`: A bad actor can steal funds by tricking the user and sending transaction bytes in place of data bytes and get a valid signed transaction which will be accepted by the blockchain.
- `AV2` - Repay attacks: A bad actor can ask a user to sign a message on the testnet and reuse the same signature on the mainnet.

To prevent `AV1`, this document proposes two guardrails on signing process: 1) prover must hash the data bytes and use the output to sign/verify instead of using data bytes directly (which will also help with `R3`), and 2) prefix the hash to be signed/verified with a `0x0` byte.

To avoid `AV2`, the network type code should be included after the `0x0` byte.

### Pseudocode Signing Implementation

```ts
const bytes = concat(
  0x0, // transaction invalidator byte
  Network.Mainnet, // network type
  blake2b256(dataBytes) // hashed data bytes
);

const signatureBytes = sign(bytes, privateKey);
```

### Why prefix it with `0x0`?

In the current transaction binary serialization format, every transaction should start with a `VLQ`[^1] value representing the number of inputs a given transaction is spending. Knowing that it's impossible to spend a transaction without inputs, it's safe to assume that a valid serialized transaction will never start with `0x0`, so this will invalidate any transaction bytes that might eventually be sent to be signed as data. Something similar happens on Ethereum, where every message to be signed must be prefixed with `0x19`[^2].

[^1]: Variable-length quantity: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable-length_quantity
[^2]: Ethereum EIP-191 specification: https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/blob/master/EIPS/eip-191.md#specification

title: ergoplatform/eips — Overview
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: ergoplatform, eips, core-protocol, markdown
# Category: ecosystem | Difficulty: intermediate

## Overview

The **Ergo Improvement Proposals (EIPs)** repository is the canonical, structured reference for all standards governing the Ergo Platform. It serves the same function as EIPs in Ethereum or BIPs in Bitcoin: a disciplined, peer-reviewed process for proposing, debating, and ratifying changes or conventions that affect the protocol, tooling, wallet integrations, and dApp development practices. Each EIP is a self-contained Markdown document with a defined format covering motivation, specification, and rationale, making the repository the authoritative source of truth for anyone building on or extending the Ergo ecosystem.

The scope of EIPs deliberately spans multiple layers of the stack. Some EIPs define **core protocol behavior** — such as consensus-level Soft-fork rules (EIP-0027, EIP-0039) touching the Emission schedule, Autolykos block rewards, and Box creation-height invariants. Others establish **client and wallet standards** (EIP-0001, EIP-0003, EIP-0020) that govern how off-chain software communicates with nodes and signs transactions. A third category covers **dApp and contract standards** (EIP-0004, EIP-0005, EIP-0022, EIP-0024, EIP-0034) that define how Native tokens, NFTs, and ErgoScript contracts should be structured so that wallets, explorers, and front-ends can interoperate without bespoke integration work.

For developers, the EIPs repository is a prerequisite reading list. Understanding which EIPs your project touches — whether you are implementing a Headless dApp, an Off-chain bot, an EIP-12-style connector, or a Multi-stage contract — determines the interfaces, data formats, Registers conventions, and transaction-building rules your code must respect. Non-compliance with a ratified EIP typically means incompatibility with the broader ecosystem tooling.

title: ergoplatform/eips — Overview
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: ergoplatform, eips, core-protocol, markdown
# Category: ecosystem | Difficulty: intermediate

## Architecture

The repository itself has a deliberately flat, document-centric architecture. There are no build artifacts, compiled outputs, or runtime dependencies — the entire content is Markdown files plus a README index. The design reflects the nature of a standards body: the "components" are the EIPs themselves, organized by concern, and their relationships are cross-references between documents.

### Logical Groupings

| Layer | EIPs | What They Define |
|---|---|---|
| **Core Protocol** | EIP-0027, EIP-0039 | Soft-fork rules, Emission retargeting, Monotonic Box creation height rule, Difficulty adjustment side-effects |
| **Wallet & Key Management** | EIP-0001, EIP-0003, EIP-0019, EIP-0044 | Application-Friendly Wallet API, Deterministic Wallet Standard (HD paths), Cold Wallet Protocol, Arbitrary Data Signing Standard |
| **Transaction Protocols** | EIP-0020, EIP-0025, EIP-0031, EIP-0043 | ErgoPay Protocol, Payment Request URI, Babel Fees, Reduced Transaction format |
| **Token & Asset Standards** | EIP-0004, EIP-0021, EIP-0024, EIP-0034 | Assets standard (Token ID rule, Registers layout), Genuine token verification, Artwork Standard, NFT Collection Standard |
| **Contract Standards** | EIP-0005, EIP-0006, EIP-0017, EIP-0022 | Contract Template format, Informal Smart Contract Protocol Specification, Proxy Contracts, Auction Contract |
| **Process** | EIP-0001 (meta), EIP-0002 | EIP formatting expectations, Ergo grant program |

### Data Flow Through the Standards

```
Core Protocol EIPs
        │  define consensus rules, Box validity, emission
        ▼
Node / Ergo Reference Client
        │  exposes REST API shaped by
        ▼
EIP-0001 (Wallet API) ──► EIP-0020 (ErgoPay) ──► EIP-0025 (Payment URI)
        │
        ▼
SDK / dApp layer
        │  builds Transactions using Boxes with Registers
        │  laid out per EIP-0004 / EIP-0024 / EIP-0034
        ▼
Wallet (EIP-0003 HD paths, EIP-0019 cold signing, EIP-0044 data signing)
        │
        ▼
Signed Transaction → mempool → confirmed eUTXO state
```

Each EIP is effectively a **contract between implementers**: a node implementation, a wallet, and a dApp can all be written independently and still interoperate because they share the normative text of the relevant EIPs.

---

title: ergoplatform/eips — Overview
text:
# content > reference > eips
# Tags: ergoplatform, eips, core-protocol, markdown
# Category: ecosystem | Difficulty: intermediate

## Smart Contracts

Several EIPs directly specify ErgoScript contracts or define standards that govern how contracts must be written and registered.

### EIP-0005 — Contract Template
Defines a structured format for publishing ErgoScript contract templates, including parameter declarations, ErgoTree derivation rules, and Constant segregation. Allows tooling to instantiate a contract by substituting constants without recompiling the full ErgoScript source, which is essential for reproducible ErgoTree verification.

### EIP-0006 — Informal Smart Contract Protocol Specification Format
Provides a documentation schema for describing Multi-stage contracts and State machine protocols. Specifies how to document each stage's Box structure, Registers usage, guarding ErgoScript, and valid Transaction shapes (inputs, outputs, Data inputs). This is the authoring standard used by projects like SigmaUSD and Dexy when publishing their protocol specs.

### EIP-0017 — Proxy Contracts
Specifies a Proxy Contract pattern where a user funds an intermediate Box whose ErgoScript allows a designated off-chain bot to complete a transaction on the user's behalf. Critical for dApps where the user cannot construct the full Transaction in one step (e.g., AMM order execution). Defines the spending conditions, refund paths, and the Minimum box value guarantees the proxy must preserve.

### EIP-0022 — Auction Contract
Provides a reference ErgoScript implementation and behavioral specification for on-chain English auctions over Native tokens and NFTs. Defines Registers layout (R4: seller address, R5: minimum bid, R6: auction end height, R7: bid step), valid bid Transaction structure, and the winner-claim Transaction. Serves as both a deployable contract and a standard so multiple auction front-ends can read the same on-chain state.

### EIP-0031 — Babel Fees
Specifies the contract and protocol allowing transaction fees to be paid in Native tokens rather than ERG. The Babel Fee provider posts a Box with an ErgoScript that accepts a specific Token ID in exchange for ERG, enabling fee-abstraction for end users. The EIP defines the exchange-rate encoding in Registers and the atomic Transaction structure that simultaneously satisfies the Minimum transaction fee in ERG and reimburses the provider in tokens.

### EIP-0027 — Emission Retargeting Soft-Fork
Though primarily a protocol-level EIP, it specifies the modified emission contract (a redeployment of the emission Box guarding script) that redistributes a portion of miner rewards to re-emission. Documents the Soft-fork activation mechanism, the new ErgoTree for the emission Singleton box, and the Storage rent implications.

# ErgoScript Audit Context — LLM Pitfalls & Calibration

When using LLMs to audit ErgoScript contracts, specific failure patterns emerge consistently. This reference documents observed pitfalls from real audits (including a human-reviewed LLM audit of the GluonW contracts) and provides calibration guidance.

---

title: ErgoScript Audit Context — LLM Pitfalls & Calibration
text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, audit, llm, security, calibration, semantics, probes
# Category: reference | Difficulty: advanced

## Observed LLM Audit Pitfalls

### 1. Indirect Token ID Checks

LLMs frequently miss that a token ID check exists when the token is referenced indirectly — for example, inside a tuple like `oracleBoxPoolNFT` or via a register lookup. The LLM reports "no token ID verification" when verification is actually present through a different code path.

**Before reporting:** Trace all references to the token through tuples, register lookups, and helper values.

### 2. Over-Recommending Identity Checks

LLMs tend to recommend additional identity checks (e.g., verifying ErgoTree bytes) when a singleton NFT already uniquely identifies the box. In common Ergo patterns, a box containing a specific singleton NFT cannot be faked — the NFT IS the identity.

**Before reporting:** Check if the box is already authenticated by a singleton NFT. If so, additional ErgoTree verification is redundant.

### 3. Missing Contextual Cancellation / Invariants

LLMs produce valid-sounding findings but miss that apparent issues are cancelled out by invariants. Examples:
- `_MinFee` appears on both input and output sides, so it cancels out and is not an attack vector
- A singleton token amount is known to be exactly 1 for a referenced box, so quantity checks are unnecessary

**Before reporting:** Check if the finding is neutralized by a matching constraint on the other side of the transaction.

### 4. Type Constraint Blind Spots

LLMs flag type issues (e.g., `Long` to `Int` downcast) without accounting for ErgoScript's type system constraints. For example, `Coll[]` indexing requires `Int`, making a `Long→Int` downcast unavoidable and expected — not a bug.

**Before reporting:** Verify whether the type conversion is required by ErgoScript's type system.

### 5. False-Flagging Bounded Numerics

LLMs flag theoretical numeric truncation or overflow issues without considering that the values are bounded by fixed constants. For example, flagging overflow on a variable that can only range 0–14 (because `BUCKETS = 14`).

**Before reporting:** Check if the values involved have fixed upper bounds that make overflow impossible.

### 6. Missing Optimization Tradeoffs

LLMs miss that some patterns are intentional design choices:
- `&&` can produce smaller ErgoTree than `allOf()` — this is a valid optimization, not a code smell
- `getVar` is off-chain supplied and may be intentionally flexible to support multiple UIs/backends

**Before reporting:** Consider whether the pattern is an intentional tradeoff rather than a mistake.

---

title: ErgoScript Audit Context — LLM Pitfalls & Calibration
text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, audit, llm, security, calibration, semantics, probes
# Category: reference | Difficulty: advanced

## Settled Semantics (empirical, do not re-derive)

Settled on a fleet-sdk MockChain harness (fleet-sdk 0.12.0, sigmastate-js 0.4.6) during the
ErgoDEX engagement, 2026-09-17 to 2026-09-20. These are probe results, not inferences, and
each has already flipped at least one real finding's verdict.

**Arithmetic and indexing fail closed, they do not fail open.**

- An out-of-range `Coll` index (`box.tokens(i)` where `i >= tokens.size`) THROWS and the whole
  script fails, including when the read sits inside an untaken `if` arm. A `tokens.size >= n`
  guard makes the same script pass. `getOrElse` returns the default.
- `Long * Int` and `Long * Long` overflow THROW ("long overflow"). The same product taken
  `.toBigInt` first does not overflow.
- `BigInt` division by zero THROWS ("BigInteger divide by zero").

Consequence: a finding whose impact depends on one of these silently producing a wrong value
is wrong as written. The transaction does not exist. Rate the denial of service, not the theft.

**`getOrElse` on a register rescues only the ABSENT register.**

`box.R4[Int].getOrElse(0)` against a box whose R4 is present but of another type THROWS
("Cannot getReg[Int](4): invalid type of value ... at id=4"). The default is supplied for
`None` only.

- A "fails open to the default" finding against a wrong-typed register is therefore usually
  WRONG: the read fails closed instead.
- A box whose own script reads `R4[Int]` unconditionally is UNSPENDABLE BY ANYONE if its R4 is
  wrong-typed. That is a full shield and it is worth crediting before rating a dependent
  contract's register read.
- A refund arm's reachability must be argued from who controls the box layout, not from the
  read being throw-safe.

**`getMany` returns a repeated key repeatedly.** A collection taken from a context variable
and passed to `getMany` without a distinctness check yields duplicate entries, so a per-entry
sum or payout can be satisfied more than once by one real entry. This is the origin of trap T8.

**Two harness caveats, so a clean probe is not mistaken for a safe contract.**

- A MockChain PASS does not prove node validity on value. MockChain does not enforce the node's
  min-value-per-byte rule: an output of 59,999 nanoERG executes there although a token-free
  P2PK box needs about 60,000. Confirm with the node's `POST /transactions/check`, or compute
  the minimum from the serialized size.
- `TransactionBuilder.from([...])` runs an input selector that SILENTLY DROPS listed inputs the
  outputs do not need, so a script box may never be spent and every script appears to pass,
  including `sigmaProp(false)`. Pass `{ ensureInclusion: true }` and assert `tx.inputs.length`
  before trusting any probe result.

---

# content > reference > ergoscript

## How to Use Audit Findings

1. **Treat LLM audit findings as hypotheses** — verify each against the ErgoScript Language Specification (LangSpec) and the actual on-chain constraints.

2. **Test off-chain assumptions** — when a finding depends on off-chain transaction construction, explicitly ask: "Can a different backend construct a transaction that violates this assumption while still satisfying the script?"

3. **Call out uncertainty** — when in doubt, flag findings as "potential" rather than "confirmed." State the conditions under which the finding would be exploitable.

4. **Cross-reference against known issues** — check each finding against the Known ErgoScript Security Issues checklist to ensure completeness.

text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, audit, llm, security, calibration, semantics, probes
# Category: reference | Difficulty: advanced

## Agent Behavior Rules for Auditing

When auditing ErgoScript contracts:

1. Verify **all spend paths** — enumerate every branch in the script's boolean logic
2. Check **invariants across state transitions** — verify that state changes maintain protocol rules
3. Verify **token and ERG conservation** — all value must be accounted for in OUTPUTS
4. Validate **signature gating** — ensure proper authentication on all spending paths
5. Ensure **predictable HEIGHT usage** — check for off-by-one errors and mempool tolerance
6. Detect **OR-branch bypasses** — test each OR branch independently for unintended spending
7. Check for **front-running vulnerabilities** — identify where sensitive data is revealed in the spending transaction
8. Verify **data input validation** — ensure data inputs are authenticated, not just assumed

# ErgoScript Audit Program

These tools run **once per contract, never on several contracts concatenated** — the
matched-docs are a semantic search on one contract's patterns, and bundling dilutes the
match and overflows the input. One `audit_contract` and one `audit_verify` per contract.

This is the working checklist for a contract audit. It is injected into both audit
passes so that Pass 1 and Pass 2 test the same population, answer the same traps, and
rate on the same matrix. The full engagement method (phases, workpapers, dual-pass
adjudication, delivery, retest) is the `contract-audit-engagement` skill.

title: ErgoScript Audit Program — Procedures, Traps, and Severity Matrix
text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, audit, security, severity, traps, debit-side, procedures
# Category: reference | Difficulty: advanced

## The principle: audit the debit side

Value under a contract leaves only when a guarded box is spent, and the script is the
sole approval control over that spend. So the audit population is every (box, spend
path) pair. For each one, answer the five questions an auditor asks of a cheque:

| Cheque question | eUTXO question |
|---|---|
| Who approved it? | Who can build a valid spending tx: signature, or permissionless with conditions? |
| Who is the payee? | Is every value-carrying output's script pinned, or is the recipient builder-chosen? |
| Is the amount right? | Rounding, overflow, integer division, unit mismatch, sum conservation? |
| Does it reconcile? | Inputs minus script-pinned outputs = residual. Who gets the residual? |
| Recorded so it can't be paid twice? | Is the state update (AVL remove, register advance, successor box) enforced on *this* path? |

Paths that create a claim (deposit, register, mint) are the credit side: confirm the
matching value actually arrived and the claim is bounded by it. Everything else is
presentation.

title: ErgoScript Audit Program — Procedures, Traps, and Severity Matrix
text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, audit, security, severity, traps, debit-side, procedures
# Category: reference | Difficulty: advanced

## Assumptions and omissions

Every protocol works under assumptions: initial state, invariants across transitions,
which actors are honest and in what proportion, what off-chain parties keep doing.
Some are enforced by a line; some hold only because the developer expects them to.
Obtain them from the developer before fieldwork and put them in a register with:
enforced by (`file:line`) or **unenforced**, compensating control, what breaks if it
fails, and how easily it fails (one actor / k actors / proportion / honest liveness
failure). Test inside the assumptions first, so a scenario that needs an assumption to
fail is not reported as if reachable. Then remove each easy-to-fail row and re-test.

In eUTXO, **every check a script does not make is a decision.** Intentional omissions
go in the register with the developer's reason; verify it against the code (cite the
line that makes the omitted check redundant, or the cost that makes it unaffordable).
An omission with neither is a finding under Completeness.

title: ErgoScript Audit Program — Procedures, Traps, and Severity Matrix
text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, audit, security, severity, traps, debit-side, procedures
# Category: reference | Difficulty: advanced

## Procedures

Run every debit-side procedure on every spend path of every fund-holding box. Record
each as **done** (line cite), **exception** (finding), or **N/A** (reason).

### Debit side (per spend path)

| # | Procedure | Assertion |
|---|---|---|
| D-1 | **Authorization.** Who can build a valid spending tx? If permissionless, list the conditions and confirm they are not trivially satisfiable. | Rights & Obligations |
| D-2 | **Self-identification.** Does the script pin its own input (`SELF.id == INPUTS(i).id`, `selfBoxIndex`)? If it assumes `INPUTS(0)` is itself, can a builder place a decoy there? | Existence |
| D-3 | **Counterparty identification.** Every input and data input read: pinned by NFT, by script hash, or only by position? | Existence |
| D-4 | **Payee pinning.** Every output carrying value out: script constrained? Recipient from trusted state, or from a builder-supplied context var? | Completeness |
| D-5 | **Amount.** Rounding direction, integer division, overflow reliance, unit mismatch, output sum tied to input? | Accuracy |
| D-6 | **Reconciliation.** Inputs minus pinned outputs = residual. Bounded? Who receives it? An unbounded residual to the builder is a finding. | Completeness, Accuracy |
| D-7 | **State update.** What must change so the same claim cannot be paid again, and is it enforced on *this* path, not just a sibling? | Completeness |
| D-8 | **Path selection.** Can the builder force a different branch: op byte unread, threshold flipped by an inflated sum? | Classification |
| D-9 | **Cutoff.** Every `HEIGHT` or time condition: can the window be shortened, moved, or backdated? Register bounded on both sides? | Cutoff |
| D-10 | **Duplicates.** Every collection from a context var or register: distinctness required? `getMany` returns a repeated key repeatedly. | Existence |
| D-11 | **Liveness dependence.** Does safety require someone to act within a window? Name who and the window. Floor MEDIUM. | Cutoff |
| D-12 | **Termination and lock.** Can the box reach a state with no valid spend? Refund or eviction path for stuck value? | Completeness |
| D-13 | **Front-running.** If permissionless, can a mempool observer replace an honest tx spending the same box with a hostile variant? | Existence |
| D-14 | **Lifecycle (multi-transaction).** Walk the box create → use → expire → renew → collect; a sequence of individually-valid txs can harm someone (entry slashable after expiry, registration with no renewal, singleton aging into rent) even when every single tx passed D-1..D-13. The procedure a single-pass audit most often skips. | Completeness, Cutoff |

### Credit side (per claim-creating path)

| # | Procedure |
|---|---|
| C-1 | Does the value the claim represents actually arrive in a guarded box in the same tx, and is that checked? |
| C-2 | Is the claim size bounded by the value that arrived? |
| C-3 | Can a claim be created with zero or recycled value (same box counted twice, decoy deposit)? |

### Source level (per contract)

| # | Procedure |
|---|---|
| S-1 | **Header vs enforced logic.** List every claim the header makes; verify each against code. Read the comment *after* the code. |
| S-2 | **Fix diffusion.** Every check one contract does right, every finding, every trap: search every sibling. Asymmetry is the signal. |
| S-3 | **Static test audit.** Read tests as evidence of intended tx layouts even if they cannot be run. A test placing an unconstrained box at an unrestricted position is evidence *for* a finding. Check that line numbers the tests cite still match the pinned source; stale anchors are INFO. |
| S-4 | **Instance parity.** Every deployed instance of the contract set at equal rigour, ranked by value held, not by which is the flagship. |

### Assumptions (per register row)

| # | Procedure |
|---|---|
| A-1 | Enforcing line found, or unenforced with a named compensating control, or a finding. |
| A-2 | Each intentional omission's reason verified against code: redundant (cite line) or unaffordable (cite cost), else a finding. |
| A-3 | Failure test: with this row removed, which spend paths' results change, and at what actor threshold. |

title: ErgoScript Audit Program — Procedures, Traps, and Severity Matrix
text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, audit, security, severity, traps, debit-side, procedures
# Category: reference | Difficulty: advanced

### Incentives (once, design level)

Sound scripts can still fail if the rational move for some role is one the design did
not intend. This is the fraud-risk assessment: incentive, not just opportunity.

| # | Procedure |
|---|---|
| G-1 | **Payoff table.** Per role, per path: honest play vs deviant play. Any cell where deviation pays more is a finding candidate. |
| G-2 | **Actor threshold.** Per finding: how many actors of what kind must deviate (one, k-of-n, 51% of stake, all honest keepers offline for T). One anonymous actor is the lowest bar. |
| G-3 | **Rational vs malicious.** Profitable deviation: the population is everyone, class as if permissionless. Griefing-only: cost relative to harm sets the class. "Needs a malicious actor" never lowers a cell by itself. |
| G-4 | **Permissionless incentives.** Who is paid to keep, liquidate, challenge, reset; is it enough; what if nobody does. |
| G-5 | **Adverse states.** When does rational play harm the protocol (bank run, profitable oracle manipulation, cascade, reseeding a drained pool at a chosen price). |

### Off-chain (builders and frontend, in scope by default when a UI exists)

The user signs what a builder constructed and a frontend displayed.

| # | Procedure |
|---|---|
| B-1 | Every user action maps to a builder and one contract path. Contract paths no builder constructs (refunds, exits) are stuck value in practice: M-Lock. |
| B-2 | The builder pins what the script leaves open (payee, residual). A script that lets the builder choose is safe only if every builder chooses correctly: an off-chain trust edge. |
| B-3 | Displayed equals enforced: slippage, fees, recipients, amounts, deadlines. |
| B-4 | Every server-supplied value that enters a transaction; what a compromised backend could make the user sign. |
| B-5 | Signing scope: the user signs exactly what was shown; nothing added after display. |

### Entity level (once)

| # | Procedure |
|---|---|
| E-1 | **Key inventory.** Every admin PK, whitelist, config box: single signer or multisig, mainnet variant present, what it can change. Single signer on mainnet is KEY-RISK. |
| E-2 | **Upgrade paths.** What can change, by whom, with what delay. |
| E-3 | **Off-chain coupling.** What breaks if the keeper or parameter is wrong or absent. |
| E-4 | **Build and hash pinning.** Repo builds; hash-pinning tests green *in this run*; re-pin procedure documented. |
| E-5 | **Traps.** Every trap below has an explicit verdict per contract with a line cite either way. |
| E-8 | **Cross-group composition.** Consolidate every trust edge (X assumes Y checks Z; closed by `file:line` or UNVERIFIED; how the counterparty is pinned) across all groups, then ask — over the edges alone, no source — which unverified or cross-group edges compose into an attack. Each candidate names the lines to read; settle it from source. Per-group passes see only their own end of an edge; this step sees both ends. The Dexy drain was two such edges composing. |

## Coverage check

Before fieldwork, one read-only agent on a cheap model is given only the interaction
map and the value ledger (no source) and names any box, terminal spend, or credit path
with no ledger row; each proposal is settled from source (add the row or log a
decision). The stdlib `validate-audits.py --phase {3,5,8}` then gates fieldwork
dispatch, the report, and sign-off as a hard gate.

# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, audit, security, severity, traps, debit-side, procedures
# Category: reference | Difficulty: advanced

## Pre-named traps

Every one comes from a real finding. Return a verdict per contract with `file:line`
either way. The vocabulary is fixed and the pole matters: **PRESENT** = the
vulnerability class is present; **ABSENT** = the class applies and the closing line is
cited; **N/A** = the construct does not exist in this contract; **PARTIAL** = present on
some paths, or pending a named probe. "PRESENT (enforced)" is not a verdict, and
ABSENT without a cited line is not a verdict.

title: ErgoScript Audit Program — Procedures, Traps, and Severity Matrix
text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, audit, security, severity, traps, debit-side, procedures
# Category: reference | Difficulty: advanced

| ID | Class | Check | Origin |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | Decoy input / positional index | Script reads `INPUTS(n)` / `OUTPUTS(n)` / `dataInputs(n)` without pinning the slot by NFT, script hash, or `== SELF`. | Dexy LP drain, 2026-09-07 (~288k ERG), `main.es`/`swap.es` |
| T2 | Guard + logic context-var execution | What is hashed vs executed, byte for byte; any path where guard runs without logic; absent ctx var fails closed? | Lithos 2026-09 |
| T3 | Singleton NFT conservation | Every spend path forces the NFT into a successor at the same script, pinned by propositionBytes or hash. | Lithos 2026-09 |
| T4 | AVL proofs | Digest pinned into successor; lookup proof for a different key; insert twice; flags/keyLength preserved. | Lithos 2026-09 |
| T5 | Bond / value accounting | Trace every arithmetic step across the lifecycle; any exit without a matching decrement. | Lithos 2026-09 |
| T6 | Permissionless spend driven by another box | Driver pinned by NFT not script; driver's logic constrains where the gated value goes. | Lithos 2026-09 |
| T7 | Testnet artifacts reaching mainnet | PK-gated whitelists/configs, dead testnet contracts; is there a mainnet variant at all. | Lithos K-1/K-2 |
| T8 | Terminal path lacks the sibling's state update | Non-terminal branch removes; terminal branch does not and enforces no sum conservation; ctx-var collection without distinctness. | Lithos H-1 `Payout.ergo` path 3 |
| T9 | Op byte unread on the co-spent side | A box that may only leave in counterparty op *k* never reads the counterparty's op var; escapes inside any other op. | Lithos H-2 `MinerData_Logic` |
| T10 | Late honest action backdates a window | Period boundary set from `HEIGHT` at transform; late transform collapses a protective window. | Lithos M-1 `Holding_Logic:190` |
| T11 | Unpinned value swept as residual | Extra admitted input with no pinned output, or withdrawal pins payees but not the remaining reserve; builder pockets it. | Lithos M-2; Dexy F-9 `hodlcoin.es` |
| T12 | Capacity exhaustion with no eviction | Bounded set fillable by entries that never progress; no removal path; permanent halt. | Lithos M-3 `Collateral_Mainnet` |
| T13 | Shared credential token across targets | One NFT id in N units authorises N boxes; any unit at `INPUTS(0)` satisfies every target; update tx admits extra inputs. | Dexy F-2 `bank.es:82`, `update.es:56` |
| T14 | Register bounded one way on a permissionless path | `>=` but no `<=`; spender sets far future; height-gated path frozen, no recovery. | Dexy F-3 `payout.es:70` |
| T15 | Script-preservation compare that skips bytes | `propositionBytes.slice(1, size)` leaves the header byte free; successor unspendable. Compare full bytes or hash. | Dexy F-4 `emission.es:24` |
| T16 | One branch lacks the script pin its siblings have | Siblings check successor `propositionBytes` + value floor; one branch checks tokens only. Diff successor checks across branches. | Dexy F-5 `buyback.es:54` |
| T17 | Token-weighted quorum with concentrated supply | Quorum sums token amounts; if one address holds a quorum, governance is that address. KEY-RISK. | Dexy F-6 `update.es:52` |
| T18 | Proportional redeem with no liquidity floor | Ratio-invariant fee lets a dominant holder drain to dust; supply 0 bricks mint; pool price resets for downstream consumers. | Dexy F-7 `redeem.es:35` |
| T19 | Stale trigger reads as sustained | Trigger records first height; reset needs an actor; consumers gate on `trigger < HEIGHT - T`; nobody resets. | Dexy F-8 `tracking.es:111` |
| T20 | Long arithmetic on a delta before the BigInt upcast | A product or sum of two `Long` deltas computed before `.toBigInt` overflows and throws: fail-closed, but it caps a legitimate value at a ceiling. Find the upcast point and check whether any arithmetic is done Long-first (D-5). | Lithos v2 F-039 (LithosDex; missed by both passes and the EKB tools, recovered only at retest) |
| T21 | Owner-only path proves ownership on inputs but never requires the token to survive | The path checks the caller holds the ownership token on the input side but never pins it into an output, so a resize, claim, or redeem can burn the owner's own token. Every owner-gated path must force the ownership token into a successor (D-4, D-7). | Lithos v2 F-040 (LithosDex; self-harm class, missed by both passes and the EKB tools) |

title: ErgoScript Audit Program — Procedures, Traps, and Severity Matrix
text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, audit, security, severity, traps, debit-side, procedures
# Category: reference | Difficulty: advanced

## Severity matrix

Set before fieldwork. A finding's severity is the cell it lands in. Deviations are
logged rulings, not arguments.

**Magnitude.** M-Total: all protocol-held value or a pool any user's funds sit in.
M-Pooled: bounded value belonging to someone other than the actor (other users, or a
protocol-owned box); one of several identical pools or vaults is M-Pooled unless the
attack reaches every instance in one transaction or repeats across all at no marginal
cost, which is M-Total. M-Integrity: no direct value path, but a mechanism protecting
others' value is defeated. M-Lock: value or function permanently unusable. M-Delay:
protocol function delayed or temporarily denied, bounded, no value at risk once it
resumes (distinct from the permanent M-Lock). M-Own: only the actor's own funds, or a
lock the victim's own signature creates. M-None: no value path.

**Likelihood is the actor threshold**: how many actors, of what kind, must deviate.
L-Open: one anonymous actor, ~fee cost, no precondition. L-Conditional: one actor with
a realistic state precondition. L-Costly: collusion of several, a proportion of stake
or hashrate, honest liveness failure, or a victim error first. L-Escalated: a
credential does more than the design issued it for (one unit bypasses a quorum; key
for A reaches B). L-Privileged: a key the design trusts, for the action it grants.
An honest-liveness failure is L-Costly by definition, and a precondition the shipped client cannot currently produce is L-Costly at that commit. A keeper or refresh path that was never built is such a precondition (L-Costly, launch-blocking), not a certainty that raises the cell. An attack rational only for a different population (a node-less miner, a stakeless holder) is rated for that population and named; a genuine three-way split routes to the developer. Profitable deviation means rational actors do it: class as if permissionless. A defect
with no deviating actor at all (an honest path that cannot be mined) is a reliability
failure rated by the LOW/INFO test, not by this axis, unless it disables a protection
users depend on within a window (then the liveness floor, MEDIUM).

| | L-Open | L-Conditional | L-Costly | L-Escalated | L-Privileged |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **M-Total** | CRITICAL | HIGH | MEDIUM | HIGH | KEY-RISK |
| **M-Pooled** | HIGH | HIGH | MEDIUM | HIGH | KEY-RISK |
| **M-Integrity** | HIGH | MEDIUM | MEDIUM | MEDIUM | KEY-RISK |
| **M-Lock** | HIGH | MEDIUM | MEDIUM | MEDIUM | LOW |
| **M-Delay** | LOW | LOW | INFO | LOW | INFO |
| **M-Own** | LOW | LOW | LOW | LOW | INFO |
| **M-None** | INFO | INFO | INFO | INFO | INFO |

Multiple paths: classify each, take the higher. A deploy-time coupling — a constant set once at launch and never touched again — whose failure is total and undetectable is LOW (launch-blocking): rated LOW but its checklist item cannot be signed off without evidence. A value changed in normal operation (a whitelist, a proof set, a rotating key) is not a coupling; a mismatch there is an operations state rated on its merits. A finding reachable only if a register
assumption fails carries that row and its threshold as precondition and is rated on
that threshold. Design-level (incentive) and off-chain (builder, frontend) findings are
rated on the same matrix; there is no softer scale for game-theory findings. **Modifiers:** front-runnable (note, no
change); liveness-dependent safety (floor MEDIUM); full on-chain shield verified this
audit (drop one level, floor LOW); partial shield (no change); latent, enabling state
not yet on-chain (no change). **Deployment status is a column, not a cell:** live,
latent, patched on-chain, not deployed. Never rate down because the code is not
deployed. **KEY-RISK** is the segregation-of-duties column, reported separately from
defects; launch-blocking if a single hot key on mainnet. **LOW vs INFO:** fail-closed
correctness with a one-line fix is LOW; hygiene with no behavioural effect is INFO.

title: ErgoScript Audit Program — Procedures, Traps, and Severity Matrix
text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, audit, security, severity, traps, debit-side, procedures
# Category: reference | Difficulty: advanced

## Finding format

Every finding carries: assertion violated (Existence, Completeness, Accuracy, Cutoff,
Rights & Obligations, Classification, Presentation); procedure that surfaced it;
`file:line`; kind (code / design / off-chain); magnitude class, likelihood class,
cell, modifiers; actor threshold and whether profitable or griefing-only; the register
assumption it depends on, if any; a numbered scenario
with magnitudes; who can do it and the precondition; for value findings the
reconciliation (value in, pinned out, residual, residual goes to); the smallest fix
that closes every variant; and confirmation the honest path still passes under the fix.
A finding without a constructed transaction is a hypothesis and is listed separately.

A candidate whose deciding fact is outside source or unsettled by any tool this session
is a **needs-validation record** (NV-n) with its trace, blocker, and plan and no
severity, listed in its own "Needs validation" report section, never in the findings
table. A refuted candidate is a **rejected record** (REJ-n) with the line that closed
it and the commit that line was read at; a later pass on the same code closes a
matching candidate by reference when that line is unchanged, else re-adjudicates it. A finding title never names a severity or KEY-RISK.

# ErgoScript Built-in Functions

All functions below are available globally in any ErgoScript contract without import or declaration.

# content > reference > ergoscript

## Sigma Proposition Constructors

```scala
def sigmaProp(condition: Boolean): SigmaProp
```
Lifts a `Boolean` into a `SigmaProp`. Required to combine boolean logic with cryptographic proofs.

```scala
def proveDlog(value: GroupElement): SigmaProp
```
Creates a sigma proposition for proof of knowledge of discrete logarithm (Schnorr signature).

```scala
def proveDHTuple(g: GroupElement, h: GroupElement, u: GroupElement, v: GroupElement): SigmaProp
```
Creates a sigma proposition for proof of a Diffie-Hellman tuple relationship.

```scala
def atLeast(k: Int, properties: Coll[SigmaProp]): SigmaProp
```
Threshold proposition: proven when at least `k` of the given sigma propositions are proven.

## Logical Aggregation

```scala
def allOf(conditions: Coll[Boolean]): Boolean
```
Returns `true` if **all** elements are `true`. Equivalent to chained `&&`.

```scala
def anyOf(conditions: Coll[Boolean]): Boolean
```
Returns `true` if **any** element is `true`. Equivalent to chained `||`.

```scala
def xorOf(conditions: Coll[Boolean]): Boolean
```
Returns `true` if an **odd number** of elements are `true`.

# ErgoScript Context Variables

Every ErgoScript contract executes within a transaction context. These global objects provide access to the transaction data and blockchain state.

---

title: ErgoScript Context Variables
text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, context, self, inputs, outputs, height, getvar, data-inputs
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Transaction Context

### `SELF` — Current Box

Type: `Box`

The input box whose contract is currently being evaluated. Always one of the `INPUTS`.

```scala
SELF.value              // Long — nanoERGs in this box
SELF.propositionBytes   // Coll[Byte] — this box's guard script
SELF.id                 // Coll[Byte] — unique box identifier
SELF.tokens             // Coll[(Coll[Byte], Long)] — tokens in this box
SELF.R4[Long].get       // typed register access
```

### `INPUTS` — All Input Boxes

Type: `Coll[Box]`

All boxes being spent in the current transaction. `SELF` is always a member of this collection.

```scala
INPUTS(0)               // Box — first input
INPUTS.size             // Int — number of inputs
INPUTS.exists { (b: Box) => b.value > 1000000000L }
```

### `OUTPUTS` — All Output Boxes

Type: `Coll[Box]`

All boxes being created by the current transaction.

```scala
OUTPUTS(0)              // Box — first output
OUTPUTS(0).value        // Long — ERG in first output
OUTPUTS.forall { (b: Box) => b.value > 0L }
```

### `CONTEXT.dataInputs` — Data Inputs

Type: `Coll[Box]`

Read-only reference boxes. They provide data without being spent, so many transactions can reference the same box concurrently (e.g., oracle price feeds).

```scala
val oracleBox = CONTEXT.dataInputs(0)
val price = oracleBox.R4[Long].get
```

---

title: ErgoScript Context Variables
text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, context, self, inputs, outputs, height, getvar, data-inputs
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Blockchain State

### `HEIGHT` — Current Block Height

Type: `Int`

The height of the block in which this transaction is being validated.

```scala
sigmaProp(HEIGHT > 700000)           // spendable after block 700,000
sigmaProp(HEIGHT < SELF.creationInfo._1 + 100)  // time-locked for 100 blocks
```

### `CONTEXT.headers` — Recent Block Headers

Type: `Coll[Header]`

The last 10 block headers preceding `HEIGHT`. Index 0 is the most recent.

```scala
val lastMiner: GroupElement = CONTEXT.headers(0).minerPk
val lastTimestamp: Long = CONTEXT.headers(0).timestamp
val lastDifficulty: Long = CONTEXT.headers(0).nBits
```

Each `Header` contains: `id`, `version`, `parentId`, `ADProofsRoot`, `stateRoot`, `transactionsRoot`, `timestamp`, `nBits`, `height`, `extensionRoot`, `minerPk`, `powOnetimePk`, `powNonce`, `powDistance`, `votes`.

### `CONTEXT.preHeader` — Current Block Candidate

Type: `PreHeader`

Information about the block being mined. Values depend on which miner finds the block.

```scala
val currentMiner: GroupElement = CONTEXT.preHeader.minerPk
val blockTime: Long = CONTEXT.preHeader.timestamp
val blockVersion: Byte = CONTEXT.preHeader.version
```

Fields: `version`, `parentId`, `timestamp`, `nBits`, `height`, `minerPk`, `votes`.

**Warning:** `preHeader` values are miner-dependent. A contract using `preHeader.minerPk` will behave differently depending on who mines the block.

---

title: ErgoScript Context Variables
text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, context, self, inputs, outputs, height, getvar, data-inputs
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Context Extension Variables (`getVar`)

Type: `getVar[T](tag: Int): Option[T]`

Off-chain data attached to an input at transaction construction time. Accessed by integer index (0-based) and expected type.

```scala
val key = getVar[GroupElement](0).get      // context var 0 as GroupElement
val data = getVar[Coll[Byte]](1).get       // context var 1 as byte array
val flag = getVar[Boolean](2).isDefined     // check if var 2 exists
```

Three outcomes when calling `getVar[T](id)`:

| Scenario | Result |
|----------|--------|
| Variable absent | Returns `None` |
| Variable present, correct type `T` | Returns `Some(value)` |
| Variable present, wrong type | **Script fails** |

### `executeFromVar`

Type: `executeFromVar[T](tag: Int): T`

Executes serialized ErgoTree bytes stored in a context variable. Enables MAST (Merkelized Abstract Syntax Trees) patterns where script fragments are provided at spend time.

```scala
val result: SigmaProp = executeFromVar[SigmaProp](0)
```

# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, context, self, inputs, outputs, height, getvar, data-inputs
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Common Patterns

**Self-replicating contract** — ensure output preserves the same script:
```scala
OUTPUTS(0).propositionBytes == SELF.propositionBytes
```

**Oracle price feed** — read from data input without consuming it:
```scala
val oracle = CONTEXT.dataInputs(0)
val price = oracle.R4[Long].get
sigmaProp(OUTPUTS(0).value >= price)
```

**Time lock** — restrict spending until a future block:
```scala
sigmaProp(HEIGHT >= SELF.R4[Int].get)
```

**Multi-input validation** — verify all inputs share the same script:
```scala
INPUTS.forall { (b: Box) => b.propositionBytes == SELF.propositionBytes }
```

# Known ErgoScript Security Issues

A checklist of known vulnerability categories for ErgoScript smart contracts. Use this when designing or auditing contracts to verify all logic against historical and theoretical flaws.

---

title: Known ErgoScript Security Issues
text:
# content > reference > ergoscript
# Tags: ergoscript, security, audit, vulnerabilities
# Category: reference | Difficulty: intermediate

## Vulnerability Categories

### 1. Unvalidated Data Inputs

Data inputs are read-only references consumed without being spent. If the contract does not verify the authenticity of a data input (e.g., checking for a specific NFT or known box ID), an attacker can substitute a malicious box with crafted register values.

**Mitigation:** Always verify data input identity via singleton NFT, expected ErgoTree hash, or known box ID.

### 2. Token Loss / Unpreserved Tokens

Tokens must be explicitly accounted for in all OUTPUTS. If a contract spends a box containing tokens but does not enforce their presence in outputs, tokens can be permanently lost or stolen.

**Mitigation:** Use `OUTPUTS.exists(...)` checks to enforce token preservation. Verify both token ID and quantity.

### 3. OR-Branch Bypass Paths

OR conditions (`||`) in spending logic can create unintended spending paths. An attacker may satisfy one branch of an OR condition that the contract designer did not intend to be independently spendable.

**Mitigation:** Audit each branch of every OR condition independently. Ensure no branch provides an unintended escape route.

### 4. Missing Signature Requirements

Contracts that do not properly gate spending with signature verification can be spent by anyone.

**Mitigation:** Use `sigmaProp(proveDlog(...))` or `atLeast(n, Coll(...))` patterns. Verify signature requirements on all spending paths.

### 5. Point-at-Infinity / Sigma-Protocol Edge Cases

The point at infinity in elliptic curve cryptography can create edge cases in Sigma protocol operations. A `GroupElement` that is the identity element can make `proveDlog` trivially satisfiable.

**Mitigation:** Validate `GroupElement` values stored in registers. Be cautious with cryptographic operations on untrusted inputs.

### 6. Missing Commit-Reveal (Front-Running)

If a contract reveals sensitive information (e.g., a secret value or decision) in the spending transaction itself, miners or observers can front-run the transaction by seeing it in the mempool.

**Mitigation:** Use the CommitReveal pattern — hash the commitment in stage 1, reveal in stage 2 in a separate transaction.

### 7. Incorrect HEIGHT Comparisons

Block HEIGHT logic is susceptible to off-by-one errors and mempool timing issues. Ergo's `CleanupWorker` re-validates mempool transactions against the new HEIGHT when a block arrives, which can cause HEIGHT-dependent scripts to fail if the tolerance window is too tight.

**Mitigation:** Use tolerance windows (e.g., `±10` blocks rather than `±1`) for HEIGHT comparisons. See the Plasma-AVL Phase 2.4-2.6 patterns for a detailed case study.

### 8. Cyclic Script Hash Dependencies

If contract A's ErgoTree references contract B's hash, and contract B references contract A's hash, neither can be deployed — a chicken-and-egg problem.

**Mitigation:** Use singleton NFTs for identity rather than script hash comparisons. Or use a factory pattern where one contract is deployed first and its hash is embedded in the second.

### 9. Scripts Too Complex Hitting Cost Limit

ErgoScript evaluation has a JIT cost budget. Complex scripts with deep nesting, large `fold` operations, or extensive collection manipulation can exceed the cost limit and fail to execute.

**Mitigation:** Keep scripts efficient. Profile JIT costs during testing. Break complex logic across multiple contract stages if needed.

---

| **CommitReveal** | Hash commitment in stage 1, reveal in stage 2 |
